source.title: Structure and dynamics of reentrant nematics: Any open questions after almost 40 years?

accepted.question_text: Across liquid-crystal systems that show a reentrant nematic (RN) phase—a nematic phase that appears again at lower temperature after a smectic phase—what microscopic mechanisms cause reentrancy in the different classes of systems, and how can those mechanisms be experimentally identified and distinguished, given that reentrancy is not caused by a single mechanism but by many?
accepted.context_brief: Microscopic mechanisms of reentrant nematic behavior

evidence.quote: The N phase at lower T was termed reentrant nematic (RN).
A main problem identified here is that reentrancy is not caused by a single microscopic mechanism, but rather by many. Their identification is still an open question.
The reason is that different microscopic mechanisms may be responsible for reentrancy in different LC systems depending on the details of the intermolecular interaction potential.

accepted.question_text: For a liquid-crystal material that has both a conventional nematic (N) phase at higher temperature and a reentrant nematic (RN) phase at lower temperature, are the N and RN phases structurally or dynamically distinct, and if so what measurable structural and dynamical observables distinguish them?
accepted.context_brief: Structural and dynamical distinction between N and RN phases

evidence.quote: a N phase formed at T above the S phase (which is usual), but also at T below the S phase (which is surprising). The N phase at lower T was termed reentrant nematic (RN).
A question naturally arising is whether RN and N phases are different. One can consider two aspects: structure and dynamics.

accepted.question_text: How does the nematic orientational order parameter Q change when a liquid crystal crosses from a smectic-A (SA) phase, in which molecules organize in layers, into a reentrant nematic (RN) phase, and can experiments resolve whether Q increases sharply, changes only subtly, or shows no enhancement?
accepted.context_brief: Nematic order across the SA-RN transition

evidence.quote: The most commonly encountered phases are nematic (N), where the system has a preferential orientation given by the nematic director, but the centers of mass have no long-range correlation; smectic (S), where molecules organize in layers.
The structure of RN's also poses some unanswered questions. For example, is there a change in nematic order parameter Q at the transition from S to RN?
Nonetheless, the question still lingers: What is the behavior of the nematic order across the S-RN phase transition?
How does the nematic order change upon crossing the SA-RN transition?

accepted.question_text: In liquid crystals whose smectic-A phase is a bilayer or partial-bilayer phase formed by antiparallel dipolar molecular pairs or dimers, is increasing frustration of the dipolar or dimer network really the microscopic mechanism that breaks the smectic layering and produces the reentrant nematic phase at lower temperature?
accepted.context_brief: Frustration mechanism in bilayer smectic reentrancy

evidence.quote: Hence, a bilayer S phase forms. As T is lowered positional order arises that leads to increasing frustration and to the breaking of the dimers. As a consequence a nematic phase appears again.
The scenario of frustrated dipolar interaction (commonly referred to as 'spin-gas theory') has played a major role in understanding different instances of reentrancy in LC.
Is frustration really the mechanism underlying the reentrant behavior in LC's with a bilayer S phase?

accepted.question_text: For liquid crystals that exhibit reentrant nematic phases without forming dimers—for example single-component, terminal-nonpolar molecules whose smectic layer thickness equals the molecular length—what experimental microscopic mechanism drives the loss of smectic layering and the return to a nematic phase?
accepted.context_brief: Mechanism of reentrancy without dimer formation

evidence.quote: Importantly, their X-ray measurements showed that the thickness of the S layers is equal to the average molecular length. Hence, dimerization cannot take place in these nonpolar compounds and the occurrence of a RN phase must have a different physical origin.
RN phases have also been observed in nonpolar substances. Dowell devised a lattice theory for a single component system that focuses on molecular chain flexibility.
Experimentally, what is the mechanism driving reentrancy in LC's that do not form dimers?

accepted.question_text: In simulations or model systems where reentrant nematic behavior appears for parallel hard-core ellipsoids with fixed molecular long-axis directions and a square-well attraction, does the reentrant nematic phase survive when orientational fluctuations and rotational dynamics of the molecules are included?
accepted.context_brief: Robustness of simulated RN phases to orientational fluctuations

evidence.quote: They considered a single-site molecular model for mesogens, where molecules are represented by parallel hard-core ellipsoids with a spherically symmetric square well potential (around each molecular long axis). In that study a RN phase and two tricritical points are found.

Though the system of parallel hard-core ellipsoids offers a clear picture of the origin of reentrancy in nematics, it has the shortcoming of neglecting rotational dynamics altogether, because the molecular long axes point in the same fixed direction. Suppressing orientational dynamics leaves open the question of whether the RN in such simple models is robust against orientational fluctuations.

accepted.question_text: Do reentrant nematic phases in single-component, nonpolar molecular liquid crystals exhibit the very large self-diffusivity along the nematic director n that simulations predicted for confined reentrant nematics, and can experiments establish translational diffusion—not another relaxation mechanism—as the cause of the observed dynamical signatures?
accepted.context_brief: Experimental status of enhanced RN self-diffusivity

evidence.quote: Figure 6 shows a dramatic increase of D∥ as one enters the RN phase whereas lower-pressure (I, N, or SA) phases exhibit rather small self-diffusivity.

However, this remains speculative, until experiments prove that translation diffusion is the main relaxation mechanism at this T. Stronger evidence is found in the conductivity experiments performed by Ratna.
Do RN phases of single-component, nonpolar molecules really exhibit the huge self-diffusivity in the direction of n̂ predicted by our simulations [12, 13]?
At the time of writing some experimental evidence exists suggesting that last question may indeed have a positive answer.

trace.notes: Resolved the arXiv abstract URL to the exact PDF, extracted the visible title, section hierarchy, terminology index, equation and figure index, and likely open-question regions on pages 3, 6, 8-9, 14, 18, 21, and 22.
Extracted the introductory open problem that reentrancy has multiple microscopic mechanisms whose identification remains open.
Extracted broad and specific questions about whether N and RN phases differ and how the nematic order parameter behaves through the S/SA-RN transition.
Extracted mechanism questions for bilayer/dimer systems, non-dimer systems, and model robustness under orientational fluctuations.
Extracted the four explicit conclusion questions and supporting context about unresolved structural and dynamical details of RN phases.
Expanded the broad mechanism-identification problem by inlining the meaning of RN and the paper's statement that multiple mechanisms are responsible for reentrancy.
Rewrote the source question about whether RN and N phases are different as a self-contained structural-and-dynamical comparison problem.
Expanded the nematic-order question with definitions of nematic and smectic phases and preserved the conflicting experimental alternatives stated in the source.
Resolved the conclusion's bilayer-smectic frustration question using the spin-gas mechanism discussion on page 12.
Resolved the conclusion's non-dimer mechanism question using the history and theory discussion of terminal-nonpolar compounds and chain-flexibility models.
Kept the simulation robustness question as distinct because it concerns a modeling assumption rather than the experimental mechanism questions in the conclusion.
Merged the conclusion's self-diffusivity question with the simulation and experimental-caveat passages so the standalone question names the needed observable and uncertainty.

Merged repeated occurrences of the nematic-order question into q_003 and repeated dynamics/self-diffusivity passages into q_007; retained q_001 as the broad mechanism-identification problem distinct from q_004 and q_005.

Did not accept the candidate 'What is the relation between the RN phase found in this simulated confined fluid and the bulk RNs?' because the same paragraph answers it by stating that the phase diagram is qualitatively similar and the structures are very similar.
Did not accept the candidate 'Why is the diffusivity so large in the direction of the long molecular axis?' because the following source text answers it through the levitation-effect analogy.

All accepted questions are self-contained, avoid source-pointing language, include page-numbered evidence, and are not marked solved by the source; therefore meta.is_solved is false for each accepted item.
